papers.title: Prevalence, etiology, and trajectory of anemia in pediatric inflammatory bowel disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Miotto D, Grunewald S, Shehan T
papers.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Anemia is a common extraintestinal manifestation of pediatric inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), yet reported prevalences vary widely, partly because case definitions differ, and no pediatric pooled estimate exists. We aimed to quantify the prevalence, etiologic composition, severity, and 1-year trajectory of anemia in pediatric IBD under age/sex-specific criteria. We searched six databases from inception to 15 June 2026 for studies in patients under 18 years. The prespecified primary analysis estimated prevalence at diagnosis in representative cohorts using World Health Organization (WHO) age- and sex-specific hemoglobin thresholds; a comprehensive estimate combined all eligible cohorts regardless of definition. Proportions were pooled by random-effects generalized linear mixed models; heterogeneity was summarized by I2 and prediction intervals. Sixty-three cohorts (15,994 children) gave an overall prevalence of 61.7% (95% CI 56.4-66.7); in the 10 WHO-defined primary cohorts (2559 children), it was 60.8% (52.5-68.4, 95% prediction interval 31.9-83.6). Prevalence varied nearly 28 points on definition alone (40.5% with fixed cutoffs vs 68.9% with age-appropriate criteria). Among anemic children, iron deficiency predominated (78.0%; five cohorts, very low certainty). Prevalence was similar in Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, higher in active disease (74.8% vs 48.5%), and fell to 37.0% at 1 year.
CONCLUSION: These definition-standardized estimates quantify a burden guidelines recognize: averaged across heterogeneous settings, two-thirds of children anemic at diagnosis, mostly from iron deficiency, and more than a third at 1 year. Because the case definition, not setting, was a significant source of variation, age- and sex-specific thresholds are essential for screening, management, and comparable research.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420261436312. Reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement.
WHAT IS KNOWN: • Anemia is a common extraintestinal manifestation of pediatric IBD, but reported prevalence ranges from about 40% to 80% and no pediatric-specific pooled estimate exists.
WHAT IS NEW: • This first pediatric-specific meta-analysis provides pooled, WHO age/sex-standardized reference estimates: in 63 cohorts (15,994 children), two-thirds were anemic at diagnosis and more than a third at 1 year. • The anemia case definition-not country income-was a significant, prespecified source of between-study variation; age- and sex-specific thresholds are essential for comparable estimates.

papers.title: Ileosigmoid knotting in Sub-Saharan Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ileosigmoid knotting (ISK) is a rare double-segment closed-loop intestinal obstruction in which the ileum and sigmoid colon entwine, frequently progressing to bowel gangrene within hours. Although rare worldwide, it is concentrated within the volvulus belt of which Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is a major component. No prior synthesis has quantitatively pooled the regional epidemiology, surgical management and outcomes.
METHODS: We performed a PRISMA-2020-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, AJOL and Google Scholar were searched from inception to January 2026. Original observational studies (≥ 5 patients) from any SSA country were eligible. Then it independently screened, extracted and appraised (adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale). Random-effects DerSimonian-Laird pooled proportions were generated, with subgroup, meta-regression and Egger analyses.
RESULTS: Ten studies (349 patients from six countries) met inclusion criteria (1949-2025). The pooled cohort was 79.1% male, mean age 42.9 years. Abdominal distension was near-universal (85%, I² = 0%); shock at presentation was 27% (95% CI 17-37%). Both segments were gangrenous in 68% (95% CI 54-82%) and only 12% had two viable segments. Resection with primary anastomosis was performed in 53% and Hartmann's procedure in 39%. Pooled in-hospital mortality was 20% (95% CI 8-32%; I² = 90.2%), falling from 50% pre-2000 to 11% since 2015 (p < 0.001); meta-regression confirmed a per-year decline (β = -0.035, p = 0.024, R² = 70%). Pooled anastomotic leak was 6% (I² = 13.7%).
CONCLUSION: ISK in SSA affects young-to-middle-aged rural men, with bowel gangrene present in the majority of cases. Contemporary mortality has fallen five-fold to 11% but remains unacceptable. Aggressive shock reversal, individualised intraoperative decision-making and standardised reporting are priorities.

papers.title: Evidence-based management of diverticulitis: systematic review of international guidelines
papers.authors: Seiffer S, Stilkerich A, Spagnolo A, Unruh J, Meyer H, Rademacher S
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diverticulitis is among the most prevalent gastrointestinal conditions, with rising incidence in younger adults. Randomized trials have challenged long-standing principles of management, including routine antibiotic use and indications for elective surgery. Clinical practice guidelines aim to standardize care but differ in methodology and scope. This systematic review aimed to identify where contemporary international guidelines agree, where they diverge, and on what evidence each position rests.
METHODS: Clinical practice guidelines on acute diverticulitis were identified by a systematic PubMed search (last updated September 2026) and hand-searching of society websites and reference lists. Articles were independently screened against prespecified eligibility criteria (explicit evidence and recommendation grading; publication in English or German; comprehensive coverage), with disagreements resolved by consensus. Recommendations were extracted into five predefined domains (classification, diagnosis, therapy of acute diverticulitis, elective surgery, long-term management) and mapped onto unified evidence and recommendation scales for direct comparison across heterogeneous grading systems. The methodological quality of each guideline was appraised using AGREE II.
RESULTS: Of 148 records identified, 146 were screened and 142 were excluded; four guidelines met the eligibility criteria, namely those of the German Society of Gastroenterology, Digestive and Metabolic Diseases/German Society of General and Visceral Surgery (Germany, 2021), the European Society of Coloproctology (Europe, 2020), American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons (USA, 2020), and the World Society of Emergency Surgery (international, 2020). All four reached consensus on fundamental principles, including selective antibiotic omission in uncomplicated diverticulitis, size-based abscess management, and individualized indications for elective surgery. Substantial discrepancies were identified in classification, the role of ultrasound, criteria for outpatient management, abscess size thresholds, indications for primary anastomosis versus Hartmann's procedure, and long-term management. Disagreement was most pronounced in areas with limited evidence, including interventional abscess drainage, laparoscopic lavage in perforated diverticulitis, and pharmacological secondary prevention. The German guideline achieved the highest AGREE II scores in all six domains; applicability scored lowest throughout (6-19%).
CONCLUSION: Clinically relevant discrepancies persist where prospective evidence is most sparse. Heterogeneous evidence, grading, and classification systems limit cross-guideline comparison. Reducing practice variation will require harmonized definitions and prospective trials comparing divergent management strategies.

papers.title: Preoperative anastomotic response microbial subtypes (ARMS) are associated with anastomotic leakage after colorectal cancer surgery
papers.authors: Zafeiropoulou K, Zafeiropoulos H, Liu K, Zwezerijnen-Jiwa F, Petersen A, Smeets B
papers.abstract: Anastomotic leakage (AL) is a severe complication following colorectal cancer (CRC) surgery, associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Identifying predictive factors for AL may improve risk stratification and facilitate early diagnosis. In this post hoc exploratory analysis of 421 CRC patients undergoing elective resection with primary anastomosis across two international, multicentre clinical studies, we profiled their preoperative fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing. AL occurred in 28 patients (6.7%). Fecal profiling revealed a bimodal distribution of Segatella copri, which served as the foundation for our two-step stratification pipeline. In Step 1, high relative abundance of S. copri was associated with successful anastomotic healing, defining candidate anastomotic response microbial subtype 1 (ARMS-1, low risk). In Step 2, among patients with low S. copri abundance, analysis of microbial metabolic potential identified 165 KEGG orthology (KO) terms enriched in AL patients. Machine learning models trained on these KOs predicted AL with high accuracy, significantly outperforming an externally validated anastomotic leak risk calculator, and differentiating candidate ARMS-2 (medium risk) from ARMS-3 (high risk). In mice, colonization with Palleniella intestinalis, the murine homolog of S. copri, enhanced the expression of transcripts key to barrier integrity, while reducing postoperative circulating markers associated with AL in our human cohort. Overall, this study demonstrates that preoperative fecal microbiome profiling enables accurate AL risk stratification through a functional two-step pipeline and offers mechanistically plausible insights into microbial contributions to anastomotic healing.

papers.title: A narrative review of the preclinical and translational potential of Silymarin and Silibinin in colorectal cancer: molecular mechanisms, clinical evidence, and nanotechnology-based delivery strategies
papers.authors: Hassani S, Sheikhnia F, Malekinejad F, Maghsoudi H, Malekinejad H, Kheradmand F
papers.abstract: This review evaluates the pharmacological potential of silymarin and silibinin as adjuncts to colorectal cancer therapy, focusing on their molecular effects, preclinical anticancer activity, pharmacokinetic limitations, and nanoformulation-based delivery. A comprehensive literature review of in vitro CRC models, in vivo animal studies, clinical investigations, and nanotechnology-based delivery systems was conducted. Relevant studies were identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science using predefined search terms related to silymarin, silibinin, colorectal cancer, chemotherapy, and nanoformulations. In vitro investigations reveal that silymarin/silibinin inhibit proliferation via G1/S arrest, apoptosis induction, and EMT suppression, targeting Wnt/β-catenin, NF-κB, PI3K/Akt, MAPK, and TGF-β pathways; however, many effects ocurred at concentrations exceeding clinically achievable systemic exposure. In vivo chemical and genetic CRC models provide preclinical evidence of reduced tumor multiplicity, enhanced antioxidant responses, and modulation of proliferation- and apoptosis-related markers. Additionally, preclinical studies suggest that silymarin/silibinin may enhance the activity of some chemotherapy agents while mitigating treatment-related toxicity; however, these findings require clinical validation. Preclinical nanoformulations have demonstrated improved bioavailability, tumor accumulation, and therapeutic activity; however, limited pharmacokinetic, safety, and clinical translation data currently restrict their therapeutic interpretation. Available clinical studies indicate reduced chemotherapy-related adverse effects and improved treatment tolerance and quality of life; whereas evidence of direct antitumor efficacy remains limited, with insufficient evidence for objective tumor response, progression-free survival, or overall survival. Further investigation of silymarin and silibinin as CRC chemotherapy adjuncts is warranted, while clinical efficacy and the advantages of nanoformulations require confirmation in exposure-informed studies and well-designed randomized trials. Adenomatous polyposis coli is illustrated with polyps in the colon. An arrow links silymarin and silibinin to colorectal polyps and lists associated changes: increased apoptosis, cell cycle arrest and autophagy, and decreased angiogenesis and metastasis.

papers.title: Nitric oxide-centered redox regulation of immune evasion in colorectal cancer
papers.authors: Guan L, Ning C, Yang Y, Wang M, Wu B, Liu J
papers.abstract: Nitric oxide (NO) links inflammation, metabolism and immune regulation in colorectal cancer (CRC), but its effects cannot be predicted from concentration alone. This narrative review develops an NO-centered redox rheostat framework defined by cellular source, local exposure, compartment, timing and the surrounding redox environment. We distinguish CRC-specific observations from mechanisms established in other systems and from proposed connections requiring validation. CRC studies support associations between nitrosative stress and inflammation, NO-dependent tumor-initiating properties, selected redox-sensitive immune pathways and donor-associated ferroptotic cell death. However, reactive oxygen species-dependent immune effects and microbial checkpoint regulation do not by themselves establish NO causality. The ferroptosis evidence is particularly conditional: NCX4040 promotes ferroptosis-associated death in cultured CRC cells, whereas NO can also inhibit lipid peroxidation and protect macrophages from ferroptosis in other experimental settings. Microbial NO-scavenging gene expression and strain-specific genomic changes suggest additional regulation of local NO availability, without defining its magnitude in human tumors. We organize therapeutic options by their demonstrated development stage and propose a biomarker panel combining nitric oxide synthase (NOS) localization, nitrosative modifications, lipid oxidation, immune state and microbial function. Clinical implementation requires tumor-selective delivery, protection of immune and normal epithelial cells, and prospective validation of pharmacodynamic assays. NO is therefore a context-dependent regulator of immune-evasive adaptation and possible ferroptotic vulnerability, rather than a uniformly tumor-promoting signal or an established therapeutic target across CRC.
